bagratid-armenia.name: Bagratid Armenia
bagratid-armenia.summary: An independent Armenian kingdom founded by Ashot I of the Bagratuni dynasty in the early 880s, ending nearly two centuries of Arab rule; its capital Ani thrived under Ashot III.

ani.name: Ani
ani.summary: A ruined medieval city, now in Turkey, that was capital of the Armenian Bagratuni kingdom from 961 to 1045, growing to perhaps 100,000 people before being sacked by the Mongols in 1236 and later abandoned.

ashot-iii-of-armenia.name: Ashot III
ashot-iii-of-armenia.summary: King of Bagratid Armenia from 952 to 977, known as Ashot the Merciful, who moved the royal seat to Ani during Armenia's golden era.

tarhana.name: Tarhana
tarhana.summary: A dried fermented food made from grain and yogurt or milk, found across Central Asian, Southeast European and Middle Eastern cuisines; known in Greek as trahanás.

zvartnots-cathedral.name: Zvartnots Cathedral
zvartnots-cathedral.summary: A medieval Armenian cathedral near Vagharshapat, built in the 7th century and now in ruins, noted for a unique circular structure with a multifloor, domed interior.

nerses-iii-the-builder.name: Nerses III the Builder
nerses-iii-the-builder.summary: Head of the Armenian Apostolic Church from 641 to 661, nicknamed 'the Builder' for major construction projects including the cathedral of Zvartnots.

cathedral-of-mren.name: Cathedral of Mren
cathedral-of-mren.summary: A 7th-century Armenian church built between 631 and 639, in the now-abandoned town of Mren near the modern Turkey–Armenia border.

david-saharuni.name: David Saharuni
david-saharuni.summary: Armenian noble who held Byzantium's top military and princely titles over Armenia, and unusually also Syria, from 635 to 638, allied with Emperor Heraclius.

heraclius.name: Heraclius
heraclius.summary: Byzantine emperor from 610 to 641 who seized power in a revolt against Phocas, then fought long wars against Persia and the Arabs, driving the Persians from Asia Minor before losing territory to Arab conquests.

cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-aghtamar.name: Cathedral of the Holy Cross
cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-aghtamar.summary: A medieval Armenian cathedral built in 921 on Aghtamar Island in Lake Van, once the seat of its own Catholicosate, now a museum.
cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-aghtamar.source_title: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar

gagik-i-artsruni.name: Gagik I Artsruni
gagik-i-artsruni.summary: Armenian noble of the Artsruni dynasty (879/880–943) who ruled Vaspurakan, first as prince and later as King, also claiming the title King of Armenia.

vaspurakan.name: Vaspurakan
vaspurakan.summary: The eighth province of ancient Armenia, later an independent medieval kingdom centered on Lake Van, in what is now southeastern Turkey and northwestern Iran, considered the cradle of Armenian civilization.

gregory-the-illuminator.name: Gregory the Illuminator
gregory-the-illuminator.summary: Founder and first head of the Armenian Apostolic Church (about 257 to about 331), reputedly a Parthian nobleman's son who was imprisoned 14 years in a pit before converting King Tiridates III to Christianity.

tiridates-iii-of-armenia.name: Tiridates III of Armenia
tiridates-iii-of-armenia.summary: Armenian Arsacid king from about 298 to 330 who adopted Christianity as Armenia's state religion around 301, making it the first state to do so officially.

tayk.name: Tayk
tayk.summary: A historical province of the Kingdom of Armenia with eight cantons, part of Armenian kingdoms from the 2nd century BC to the 9th century AD before later passing to Georgian, then Turkish, control.

true-cross.name: True Cross
true-cross.summary: In Christian tradition, the original wooden cross on which Jesus was crucified, said to have been recovered in Jerusalem by Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, around 326–328.

nerses-kamsarakan.name: Nerses Kamsarakan
nerses-kamsarakan.summary: A prince who briefly ruled Armenia as presiding prince from 689 to 691 with Byzantine backing, appointed in place of rival Ashot II Bagratuni.

byzantine-iconoclasm.name: Byzantine Iconoclasm
byzantine-iconoclasm.summary: Two periods (about 726–787 and 814–842) when Byzantine religious and imperial authorities opposed the veneration of icons, causing civil wars and destruction of religious images.

saint-catherine-s-monastery.name: Saint Catherine's Monastery
saint-catherine-s-monastery.summary: Christian monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, Egypt, built 548 to 565 under Byzantine emperor Justinian I; the world's oldest continuously inhabited Christian monastery.

ibn-khordadbeh.name: Ibn Khordadbeh
ibn-khordadbeh.summary: A Persian bureaucrat and geographer in the Abbasid Caliphate, active in the 9th century, who wrote the earliest surviving Arabic book of administrative geography.

byzantine-lyra.name: Byzantine lyra
byzantine-lyra.summary: A pear-shaped, three-to-five-string bowed instrument from the Byzantine Empire, held upright and played with the fingertips; its descendants are still played around the Balkans and Black Sea.

rebab.name: Rebab
rebab.summary: A bowed, sometimes plucked, string instrument that spread across North Africa, West and Central Asia via Islamic trade routes; one of the earliest known bowed instruments, named by the 8th century.

bagpipes.name: Bagpipes (salandj)
bagpipes.summary: A woodwind instrument using reeds fed by air stored in a bag, played for centuries across Europe, North Africa, West Asia and northern South Asia.

khosrow-ii.name: Khosrow II
khosrow-ii.summary: Last great pre-Islamic monarch of Iran, ruling the Sasanian Empire from 590 to 628; he conquered Roman territory in the Middle East before being deposed and killed by his own son.

kavad-ii.name: Kavad II
kavad-ii.summary: Sasanian King of Kings of Iran briefly in 628, who overthrew and executed his father Khosrow II and made peace with the Byzantines, ending their long war.

cappadocia.name: Cappadocia
cappadocia.summary: A historical region of Central Anatolia in Turkey, known for its fairy-chimney rock formations and its long history as a center of early Christian monastic life.

shahrbaraz.name: Shahrbaraz
shahrbaraz.summary: A Sasanian general who seized the Persian throne in 630 CE from Ardashir III and was killed by nobles after only forty days; he had played a major role in the Byzantine-Sasanian war of 602-628.

pannonian-avars.name: Pannonian Avars
pannonian-avars.summary: A confederation of Eurasian nomads who built the Avar Khaganate in the Carpathian Basin from the late 6th to early 9th centuries, known for invasions of the Byzantine Empire and influence on Slavic migrations.

iranian-plateau.name: Iranian plateau
iranian-plateau.summary: A vast geological and historical region stretching from the Caspian Sea to the Sulaiman Mountains, including ancient Parthia, Media and Persis, and covering much of modern Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

michael-ii.name: Michael II
michael-ii.summary: Byzantine emperor from 820 to 829 and founder of the Amorian dynasty, who seized power after conspiring in the murder of his predecessor and faced a long revolt before losing Crete and Sicily.

leo-v-the-armenian.name: Leo V the Armenian
leo-v-the-armenian.summary: Byzantine emperor from 813 to 820 who ended a long war with the Bulgars and revived Byzantine iconoclasm in 815; he was assassinated by supporters of his general Michael the Amorian, who succeeded him.

thomas-the-slav.name: Thomas the Slav
thomas-the-slav.summary: A 9th-century Byzantine military commander who led a major revolt against Emperor Michael II in 821–823, briefly besieging Constantinople before his defeat.

book-of-dede-korkut.name: Book of Dede Korkut
book-of-dede-korkut.summary: The most famous of the epic dastans of the Oghuz Turks, carrying the values of nomadic Turkic pre-Islamic life and surviving today in only a few manuscripts.

oghuz-turks.name: Oghuz Turks
oghuz-turks.summary: A western Turkic people whose 8th-century tribal confederation in Central Asia became the ancestors of today's Turkmen, Azerbaijanis and Turks.

anania-shirakatsi.name: Anania Shirakatsi
anania-shirakatsi.summary: 7th-century Armenian polymath considered the father of Armenia's exact and natural sciences, writing on mathematics, astronomy, geography and chronology and compiling the earliest known arithmetic tables and math puzzles.

ashkharhatsuyts.name: Ashkharhatsuyts
ashkharhatsuyts.summary: An early medieval Armenian geographical work, written around 610 to 636 CE and usually attributed to Anania Shirakatsi, valued as a unique source on Armenia before the Arab conquests.

caucasian-albania.name: Caucasian Albania
caucasian-albania.summary: A former state in the ancient Caucasus, mostly overlapping present-day Azerbaijan, which came under Sasanian Persian suzerainty from 252 AD until the empire's fall.

trabzon.name: Trabzon
trabzon.summary: City on Turkey's Black Sea coast, founded in 756 BC by Greek colonists, later capital of the Byzantine successor Empire of Trebizond before falling to the Ottomans in 1461.

pappus-of-alexandria.name: Pappus of Alexandria
pappus-of-alexandria.summary: A Greek mathematician of late antiquity, active around 290 to 350 AD in Alexandria, best known for his eight-volume Collection covering geometry, astronomy and mechanics.

dvin-ancient-city.name: Dvin
dvin-ancient-city.summary: A large commercial city and capital of early medieval Armenia near modern Yerevan, with a population estimated at up to 100,000–150,000 at its height, before its destruction by the Mongols in the 13th century.

arabic-mile.name: Arabic mile
arabic-mile.summary: A historical unit of length, between about 1,800 and 2,000 metres, used by medieval Arab geographers and astronomers.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.

sasanian-empire.name: Sasanian Empire
sasanian-empire.summary: An Iranian empire ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD, founded by Ardashir I to revive the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire; at its height it stretched from Egypt to Central Asia.

perpetual-peace-532.name: Treaty of Eternal Peace
perpetual-peace-532.summary: A 532 treaty between the Byzantine and Sasanian Persian empires ending the Iberian War, bringing relative peace between them until fighting resumed in 540.

kingdom-of-iberia.name: Kingdom of Iberia
kingdom-of-iberia.summary: The Greco-Roman name for the Georgian kingdom of Kartli, centered on eastern Georgia, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century before falling under Persian and later Byzantine influence.

lazica.name: Lazica
lazica.summary: An ancient kingdom in what is now west Georgia, formed after the collapse of Colchis and gaining independence around 131 AD.

sasanian-armenia.name: Sasanian Armenia
sasanian-armenia.summary: The portion of Armenia under Sasanian Persian control, especially after 428 CE when the Armenian kingdom was abolished and replaced by governors called marzbans, lasting until the Arab conquest in the 7th century.

barda-azerbaijan.name: Partav
barda-azerbaijan.summary: The old name of Barda, a city in Azerbaijan that became capital of Caucasian Albania by the late 5th century and remained the region's chief city into the 10th century.

varaz-grigor.name: Varaz Grigor
varaz-grigor.summary: The first known Mihranid king of Caucasian Albania, ruling from 628 until at least 654.

hellenizing-school.name: Hellenizing School
hellenizing-school.summary: An Armenian intellectual movement of the 5th to 8th centuries devoted to translating Greek texts into Armenian, shaping the language and preserving some Greek works otherwise lost.

paulicianism.name: Paulicianism
paulicianism.summary: A Christian sect that originated in Armenia in the 7th century, flourishing along the Byzantine–Arab frontier until its state at Tephrike was destroyed by the Byzantines in the 870s.

constantine-silvanus.name: Constantine-Silvanus
constantine-silvanus.summary: Founder of the Paulicians, a 7th-century Armenian Christian movement seeking to return to the early church of Paul the Apostle; he was eventually stoned to death on imperial orders.

samsat.name: Samosata
samsat.summary: A town on the upper Euphrates in Turkey, formerly called Samosata, which served as the ancient capital of the Kingdom of Commagene.

maximus-the-confessor.name: Maximus the Confessor
maximus-the-confessor.summary: Christian monk, theologian and Neoplatonic scholar (c. 580-662) who served Byzantine Emperor Heraclius before entering monastic life; persecuted and mutilated for insisting Christ had both a human and divine will, he died in exile in Georgia.

tsageri.name: Tsageri
tsageri.summary: Small town in western Georgia, on the Tskhenis-Tsqali river, where the theologian Maximus the Confessor died in exile in 662.

gregory-of-narek.name: Gregory of Narek
gregory-of-narek.summary: An Armenian mystical poet, monk and theologian (about 950 to 1003 or 1011), son of a bishop, considered the most significant figure in Armenian religious literature and named a Doctor of the Church by Pope Francis in 2015.

narekavank.name: Narekavank
narekavank.summary: A tenth-century Armenian monastery near Lake Van where the poet Gregory of Narek lived and worked, abandoned in 1915 during the Armenian genocide and later demolished.

lake-van.name: Lake Van
lake-van.summary: Turkey's largest lake, a saline soda lake in the Armenian highlands with no outlet, formed after a volcanic eruption blocked its original drainage.

tondrakians.name: Tondrakians
tondrakians.summary: An anti-feudal Christian sect in medieval Armenia, active from the early 9th to 11th century around the district of Tondrak near Lake Van.

council-of-manzikert.name: Council of Manzikert
council-of-manzikert.summary: A 726 council that reconciled the Armenian and Syriac Orthodox churches, affirmed Christ as a single nature, and formally withdrew the Armenian church from communion with the Greek Orthodox church.

divri-i.name: Divriği
divri-i.summary: Town in Sivas Province, Turkey, today known for its 13th-century Great Mosque and Hospital, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, on the site of the historic stronghold once called Tephrike.

plotinus.name: Plotinus
plotinus.summary: An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 204/5–270 AD) regarded as the founder of Neoplatonism, whose ideas on the One, Intellect and Soul influenced later religious and philosophical thought.

porphyry-of-tyre.name: Porphyry
porphyry-of-tyre.summary: A Phoenician Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305) who edited his teacher Plotinus's works and wrote an introduction to logic used throughout the Middle Ages.

iamblichus.name: Iamblichus
iamblichus.summary: A Syrian Arab Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245 – c. 325) who shaped the later direction of Neoplatonism and wrote a biography of Pythagoras.

proclus.name: Proclus
proclus.summary: A Greek Neoplatonic philosopher (412 to 485 CE) who developed one of the most elaborate systems of Neoplatonism, influencing Byzantine, Islamic, and later Western philosophy.

koine-greek.name: Koine Greek
koine-greek.summary: The common form of Greek spoken and written across the Hellenistic world, Roman Empire and early Byzantine Empire, spreading after Alexander the Great's conquests and used for the Septuagint and New Testament.

isaurian-language.name: Isaurian language
isaurian-language.summary: Extinct language spoken in Isauria, Asia Minor, attested in inscriptions into the 6th century AD, with personal names showing Luwian, Indo-European roots.

taurus-mountains.name: Taurus Mountains
taurus-mountains.summary: A mountain range in southern Turkey separating the Mediterranean coast from the central Anatolian Plateau, stretching from Lake Eğirdir to the upper Euphrates and Tigris rivers.

seljuk-dynasty.name: Seljuk dynasty
seljuk-dynasty.summary: The Oghuz Turkic, Sunni Muslim ruling family, also called the House of Seljuk, that founded the Seljuk Empire along with the Sultanates of Kermân and Rum, targets of the First Crusade.

isauria.name: Isauria
isauria.summary: Rugged, isolated district in the interior of ancient Asia Minor, home to the fiercely independent Isaurian mountain people who raided neighboring lands under Macedonian and Roman rule.

luwian-language.name: Luwian language
luwian-language.summary: An ancient Indo-European language, or group of languages, of Anatolia, written in cuneiform or hieroglyphic scripts and named after the region of Luwiya.
